rationale: This is a near-rediscovery of the archive's "Dilutive Capex Shock" (identical IND_RANK capex-shock leg, equity-issuance financing leg merely rescaled from capex to total active external financing and MIN swapped for MUL), and the stated motivation about avoiding a "split-contaminated share-count channel" is irrelevant since no share-count item appears in either version.

Both legs are already in the archive—TS_RANK capex-cycle leg from "Debt-Funded Capex Cycle Peak" and the identical short-debt-share leg from "Short-Debt Capacity Mismatch" (fmb -0.87)—so this is a mechanical recombination that swaps only the capex scaler (at→ppent) rather than a new mechanism.

Effectively a cosmetic re-parameterization of "Short-Debt Inventory Funding Mismatch" (same short-debt-share financing leg; inventory-vs-capex mix restated as a difference of asset-scaled deltas instead of a share), so it is unlikely to yield independent information about the channel.

The three-way uses-of-funds strain (capex ramp + debt issuance + dividend commitment) is genuinely new relative to the archive and internally consistent, though the dvc/at leg is a persistent level variable that tilts toward mature dividend payers whose unconditional alpha runs against the predicted negative sign, so the interaction may be diluted by a payout main effect.

This reduces to capex intensity × net long-term debt issuance—already covered by "Debt-Funded Tangible Capacity Expansion" and "Debt-Funded Capex Cycle Peak"—and the ABS(ceq) scaler is economically incoherent, since negative-book-equity firms (the most capacity-strained) get their strain measure sign-scrambled and near-zero-equity firms dominate the ranking.

This is a legitimate diagnosis-driven reinterpretation of the sign-flipped "Cash-Drawdown Capex Discipline" result (whose -3.16 alpha t-stat contradicted its positive prior) with an internally consistent expression, but it leans on the same short-debt-share leg that has repeatedly added little in the archive, so the incremental value rests mainly on the cash-depletion channel.
